title: Circle's USDC squeeze and the HKMA STR backlog hiding in plain sight
summary: Circle's stablecoin revenue war puts VASP compliance officers on notice, while Hong Kong's overdue STR quality remediation and year-end CDD deadlines demand board attention now. Alex and Jordan disagree on what the Circle story really signals for AML teams.
script:
ALEX: There is a commercial battle inside the stablecoin market right now, and I want to argue it is also a compliance story. Circle is defending its USDC revenue-sharing model against rivals offering distribution partners a bigger cut. Jordan, I think the AML read here is being missed entirely by the industry.

JORDAN: Tell me your read, because my instinct is that this is a business-model story dressed up as a compliance concern. Circle completed its public listing earlier this year, its unit economics are under analyst scrutiny, and rivals are circling. That is a corporate finance story.

ALEX: It is both, and here is why I push back on separating them. When distribution economics shift aggressively in a stablecoin market, you get a race to onboard partners faster to defend volume. Faster partner onboarding means pressure on know-your-business due diligence, on counterparty risk assessments, and on the transaction monitoring calibration that sits behind USDC flows. That is squarely an AML concern.

JORDAN: Right, but I want to add a sharper edge to that. The compliance risk is not just at Circle. It is at every virtual asset service provider that distributes USDC or holds it in customer wallets. If the distribution economics shift, you may see smaller or less rigorous distributors gaining ground because they are willing to accept thinner margins from a different issuer. And those distributors may have weaker controls. So the deterioration in the risk profile is distributed across the ecosystem, not concentrated at one issuer.

ALEX: That is a fair point. And it connects to something regulators in this region are watching closely. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has been explicit in its digital payment token licensing conditions about counterparty risk management. When you are a licensed digital payment token service provider accepting USDC or a competitor stablecoin for settlement, your counterparty risk framework needs to account for issuer stability and the distribution chain integrity, not just the on-chain mechanics.

JORDAN: So what should listeners do with this? If you are the compliance officer or MLRO at a virtual asset service provider in Singapore, Hong Kong, or Australia, this is the moment to pull your stablecoin counterparty risk assessment and ask whether it was written when Circle had a different commercial profile. A pre-IPO Circle looked different from a publicly listed Circle under analyst pressure. The risk assessment should reflect current facts. That is a specific artefact to update before your next risk committee.

ALEX: And for AUSTRAC-regulated entities in Australia, this maps directly to the customer risk assessment requirements under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act. If stablecoin issuers or distributors are in scope as designated service providers within your customer base, those risk ratings need to reflect the current competitive and commercial environment. Not a theoretical one.

JORDAN: Agreed. Though I will say, I think regulators in this region have been slower than the commercial reality here. The MAS licensing framework is rigorous, but the guidance on issuer-level counterparty risk for stablecoin distributors is thinner than it should be given how fast this market is moving.

ALEX: That is a fair supervisory criticism. Let me take us to Hong Kong, because there is an obligation sitting on desks right now that I suspect is getting crowded out by end-of-year noise. The HKMA's STR quality thematic review from the fourth quarter of last year resulted in deficiency letters going to roughly a quarter of authorised institution population in early 2026. Closure of those findings is still a live obligation for firms that received letters.

JORDAN: And I want to be direct about what "closure" means in practice, because I think some firms are treating it as a correspondence exercise rather than a remediation exercise. Closing a deficiency finding from an HKMA thematic review means demonstrating that the underlying control has changed, not that you wrote a letter explaining why your current approach is adequate. The HKMA has been clear in its supervisory communications that STR narrative quality is about the information density of the narrative, the articulation of the predicate offence, and the timeliness linkage between trigger event and filing. If your remediation plan addresses process documentation but not the actual quality of STR narratives coming out of your operations team, you have not closed the finding.

ALEX: And the September thirtieth deadline for the annual AML and CFT self-assessment return under HKMA guideline eleven has just passed. So firms that are behind on STR remediation and have just submitted a self-assessment are now in a position where the two things need to be consistent. If you told the HKMA in your self-assessment that STR quality is now well-controlled, the evidence behind that claim needs to hold up.

JORDAN: That is a really important point and I do not think it is being talked about enough. The self-assessment and the thematic remediation are being managed in parallel in a lot of institutions, sometimes by different teams, and the outputs are not always reconciled before submission. If I were an examiner, that is exactly where I would look first.

ALEX: So the action here is specific. If you are the MLRO at an HKMA-authorised institution that received a deficiency letter earlier this year, before you close out October, sit your team down and cross-reference what you stated in your self-assessment return against the actual remediation evidence. If there is a gap, raise it internally now rather than wait for the next examination cycle to surface it.

JORDAN: And on the December thirty-first deadline for periodic customer due diligence review of high-risk customers under section sixteen of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, which is the AMLO, that is ten weeks away. If your high-risk customer population is large and your review cadence has slipped, ten weeks sounds like enough time and frequently is not. Get a count now of open reviews and make sure the resourcing is committed.

ALEX: What to watch into the rest of this week: the commercial pressure in the stablecoin market will generate more noise around issuer economics, and I expect we will see supervisory commentary from at least one APAC regulator before year-end on stablecoin counterparty risk standards for licensed VASPs. Watch the MAS website for any updates to the digital payment token service frameworks.

JORDAN: And if the Hong Kong compliance calendar felt uncomfortable just now, it should. End-of-year in Hong Kong is always a crunch, but this year the STR remediation layer makes it harder than usual. Start the resourcing conversation with your head of financial crime this week, not in November. The full obligation register and source links for everything we covered today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you tomorrow.
